comments.body:
Design decision (session with operator, 2026-07-29): resolve this as part of jira-reb-1582, not independently.

Root cause confirmed by reading the resolver. resolve_hierarchy_link (src/rebar/graph/_hierarchy.py:98) defines "comparable level" by TICKET TYPE TIER (_TYPE_TIER: epic=2, story=1, task/bug=0) and promotes the lower-tier endpoint up its parent chain to the first ancestor at the higher tier. In the repro, T1 (task, tier 0) depends_on S (story, tier 1) with both as direct children of epic E: the resolver looks for a tier-1 (story) ancestor of T1, walks the chain [T1, E], finds none (E is tier 2), and hits the chain-root fallback at _hierarchy.py:93 -- returning E. Hence E depends_on its own child S.

Under jira-reb-1582s structural rule (comparability = sharing a parent, not sharing a type) this is unreachable: T1 and S are siblings, so the link records exactly as requested with no promotion. So 1803 is a symptom of the type-tier policy, and its repro becomes a regression test on the 1582 change rather than a separate fix.

Second defect found while tracing, to be fixed in the same change: add_dependency (src/rebar/graph/_links.py:180) raises on is_redundant, but is_redundant is computed by the resolver from the ORIGINAL source/target pair, before promotion. T1->S is not redundant; the promoted E->S is, and nothing re-checks it. The guard must be applied to the RESOLVED pair, and generalized from "direct parent-child" to "any ancestor/descendant" -- a hard invariant that a ticket never blocks its own subtree regardless of how the edge was produced (including via later re-parenting).

Status: no code claimed or written yet.

compiled_state.description:
## Summary
Creating a cross-level sibling `depends_on` link escalates the source up the hierarchy and can make an epic block itself (a parent gains a `depends_on` on its own child), which is nonsensical and can wedge `ready`/claim-cascade logic.

## Repro
1. Epic E with children: a `story` S (foundational) and several `task`s T1..Tn (all direct children of E).
2. Attempt to record the real dependency `rebar link T1 S depends_on` (a task depending on a higher-level story sibling).
3. Because "blocking deps (blocks/depends_on) are promoted to a comparable hierarchy level", the link source is REDIRECTED from T1 up to the parent epic E. Observed tool output:
   `{"redirected": true, "original": {"source": "T1", "target": "S"}, "resolved": {"source": "E", "target": "S"}}`
4. Net effect: the epic E now has `depends_on -> S`, i.e. E depends on its own child. The intended per-child dependency (T1 -> S) is NOT recorded.

## Expected
Either (a) record the dependency at the level requested (T1 depends_on S) without escalating past a shared ancestor, or (b) reject the link with a clear error, but NEVER produce a parent -> own-descendant blocking edge. A ticket must not end up blocking itself or its own subtree.

## Impact
- Silent: the user believes T1->S was recorded; it was not (the child is left unblocked; the parent is spuriously blocked).
- The epic becomes blocked by its own child, which can distort `ready`, `next-batch`, and the parent-first claim/transition cascade.
- Workaround used on epic 8fc2-0306-a9a0-4864: retype the lower-level children to the SAME type as the foundational ticket (all `story`) so same-level `depends_on` links persist without escalation, then `rebar unlink` the spurious epic->child edge.

## Notes
Discovered while wiring the dependency graph for the T15 plan-review-criterion epic. The escalation/promotion rule is documented in `rebar link` help ("blocking deps are promoted to a comparable hierarchy level"); the defect is that promotion can cross the parent boundary and self-reference the ancestor rather than being clamped below the nearest common ancestor.
compiled_state.title: depends_on escalation makes an epic block its own child (parent<-child self-block)
